section.title: Computer algebra systems and integral tables

introduction.p: Integral tables and computer algebra systems can suggest antiderivatives and simplify expressions. Check a proposed answer by differentiating it on the relevant domain. Pay particular attention to absolute values, branch choices, singularities, and assumptions that may be implicit in the output.

subsection.title: Equivalent antiderivatives can look different
subsection.p: Two correct antiderivatives of the same function may look different. If they differ only by a constant on an interval, they represent the same family of antiderivatives.

hint.p: If two functions have the same derivative on an interval, they differ by a constant there. Algebra can hide that constant inside logarithms or inverse trigonometric identities.

subsection.title: Branch and domain issues
subsection.p: An indefinite integral is not a global object on every part of the real line at once. It is usually a family of antiderivatives on intervals where the integrand is defined.
This matters most for logarithms, square roots, and inverse trigonometric functions.

exercise.title: Why is an indefinite integral not a global object on the whole line?

statement.p: A computer might return \ln x for \int(1/x)\,dx, which is correct only on (0,\infty). In your own words, why do logarithms, square roots, and inverse trigonometric functions force you to check the interval, and why does an absolute value still not glue two separate intervals into one antiderivative?

hint.p: An antiderivative lives on an interval where the integrand is defined. The point x=0 still splits the domain of 1/x into two pieces, each with its own constant.

subsection.p: The important question is not always “Can we find an elementary antiderivative?” Often the better question is:

p.me: \text{How accurately do we need the accumulated amount?}

subsection.p: That question leads naturally to numerical integration.

subsection.title: A responsible workflow with tools
subsection.p: When using a table or computer algebra system, work in this order.

cell.p: Inspect the integrand first. Identify possible structure.
Try a human method if the structure is clear.
Use a table or CAS to check, compare, or explore.
Check the interval, branch, and absolute values.
For a definite integral, check whether endpoints or discontinuities cause trouble.
Decide whether an exact form, special-function form, or decimal approximation is most useful.

subsection.p: The last endpoint check points toward the next section. A definite integral over a finite interval with a continuous integrand is safe. But many important integrals are not of that kind. The interval may be infinite. The integrand may blow up. A formal antiderivative may exist while the accumulated amount is not finite.

So the next question is not how to find an antiderivative. It is more basic:

p.me: \text{When does an infinite or singular accumulation have a finite value?}
